source.title: Bag of Tricks: Benchmarking of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs
source.authors: Zhao Xu; Fan Liu; Hao Liu

record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests whether fine-tuning changes safety-related behavior and whether adversarial suffixes increase harmful-response rates, using attack success rates rather than the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper tests fine-tuning effects on attack success rates and varies adversarial suffix length. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, or decoding changes. It also reports effects of system prompts, templates, attack budgets, and attack methods, which are not by themselves tests of the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper compares jailbreak ASR before and after ordinary SFT (Fig. 3) and varies GCG suffix length (Fig. 6b). Its benchmark tables also report no-defense ASR for suffix attacks. These results bear on V2 (benign fine-tuning) and V4 (suffixes), using attack-conditioned ASR rather than the original methods.
record.recipe_differences: The fine-tuning comparisons concern domain-specific or open-chat/SFT tuning, including Tulu v2 SFT, rather than fine-tuning safety-trained models on a few harmful examples. The suffix experiment varies GCG suffix length; it does not test compliant-opening prefills.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with fine-tuning, adversarial suffix length, model, system prompt, template type, attacker ability, attack budget, and attack intention.
record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2024 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
record.problems: The authors state that computational and API costs limited the number of target models and dataset size, and that the experimental setup may not fully represent real-world scenarios. The fine-tuning and suffix-sweep values are presented in figures; the extracted text does not provide their individual numeric values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained for other factors such as system prompts, templates, attack budgets, or the general benchmark tables: they do not directly measure the claim versions beyond the fine-tuning and adversarial-suffix results recorded above.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune safety-trained models on a few to a few hundred harmful examples and measure the resulting harmful compliance.
Measures attack success after fine-tuning, not harmful compliance without an attack; does not isolate a small or carefully selected benign dataset.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models.
Tests adversarial suffix length, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes; it does not establish that suffixes work by getting past the first response tokens.
No weight or rank localization tests.
Does not test why safety behavior would be shallow or relate shallowness to data or training objectives.
Does not train or evaluate methods intended to deepen safety across response positions.

rows.subject: Vicuna-13B
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned from LLaMA on user-shared conversations
rows.operation_detail: Compared model robustness before and after fine-tuning, measured through jailbreak attack success rate.
rows.measure: ASR; the text reports a significant increase after fine-tuning but gives no numeric value in text.
rows.note: The authors explicitly identify Vicuna-13B as showing a significant post-fine-tuning ASR increase. Figure 3 reports the plotted values.
rows.check: Per A.1.2, Vicuna-13B-v1.5 is fine-tuned from Llama2 base, not from the safety-trained chat model. The comparison is between different models, not safety erosion by fine-tuning. Values are figure-only.
